analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.25 over three years and expands the earned income tax credit for working families.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on this bill to step the minimum wage up from $3.35 to $4.25 and expand the earned income tax credit; it sat in committee for 17 months until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps from $3.35 an hour to $3.65 in 1990, $3.95 in 1991, and $4.25 in 1992. It would also enlarge the earned income tax credit, a tax break that puts money back in the paychecks of low-wage working families, and make it easier to receive part of that credit through paychecks during the year. To soften the cost for employers, it would let restaurants count a bigger share of tips toward the minimum wage and exempt small firms with under $500,000 in annual sales from the higher wage floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning near the minimum wage would get a raise of up to 90 cents an hour by 1992. Low-income working parents would get a larger earned income tax credit, with extra credit for each school-age or preschool child, and could receive part of it in each paycheck instead of waiting for a tax refund. Restaurant and other employers would get offsets in return: a bigger tip credit and an exemption for firms with less than $500,000 in annual sales, though newly exempt firms that were covered in 1988 would still have to pay the old $3.35 minimum [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage workers and low-income working families

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $3.35 an hour to $3.65 in 1990, $3.95 in 1991, and $4.25 in 1992 and after — a raise of up to 27% for the lowest-paid workers

Expands the earned income tax credit: earned income up to $7,000 (up from $5,714) counts toward the credit, and the credit percentage rises with the number of qualifying children, from 20% with one child to 35% with four or more, on top of the previous flat 14%

Adds extra credit for families with children — 5% more for each school-age child and 10% more for each preschool child, per the bill's summary — and indexes all credit amounts to inflation starting in 1992 so they don't erode

Expands the program that lets workers receive part of the earned income credit in each paycheck, and requires employers to collect a certificate or an ineligibility statement at hiring so more eligible workers actually sign up

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wage would bear the raise, most directly restaurants and small retail and service firms. The larger earned income tax credit would be paid for by the federal treasury — taxpayers generally. As an offset, businesses would get a tip credit rising to 50% of the minimum wage (letting employers count more of workers' tips toward the wage floor) and an exemption for enterprises under $500,000 in annual sales, though those firms would still owe the old $3.35 rate if they were covered in 1988 [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tip credit would rise from 40% to 50% of the minimum wage, meaning employers could count more of a server's tips toward the wage floor and pay less out of their own pocket — tipped workers would see less of the raise in guaranteed wages

The small business exemption would drop coverage for enterprises with annual sales under $500,000 (the threshold was $362,500), so workers at those firms would not get the increases to $3.65–$4.25 — though firms newly exempt that were covered in 1988 would still have to pay $3.35

Requiring every employer to collect a signed earned income certificate or a signed statement of ineligibility at hiring would add paperwork and compliance duties, a burden that falls hardest on small employers

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: a higher wage floor for the lowest-paid workers and a bigger, inflation-proofed tax credit for working poor families, with offsets that make the wage increase easier for small firms and restaurants to absorb. The trade-offs are genuine but modest — tipped workers would keep less of the raise in guaranteed cash wages, and some small-firm workers would be left out of the increases entirely. On balance the bill's main effect would be a transfer to low-wage workers and their families, paid for by employers and federal revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1989, split between two House committees, sent to a subcommittee a month later, and was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended — the action log's final entry simply points to a different bill, H.R. 5835.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave McCurdy introduced the bill on June 14, 1989, and it was sent jointly to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor Committees
A month later, in July 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where it sat
No committee ever reported it out and no chamber ever voted on it; the last action in the record, on November 5, 1990, says only 'See H.R. 5835', pointing to another bill that handled the subject
The bill drew just two cosponsors — one Democrat and one Republican — and never reached the floor of either chamber

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed higher wages under this version — particularly small firms and restaurant owners, who also would have faced new certificate paperwork — were better off because the bill died in committee. Minimum-wage workers and low-income working families gained nothing from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill's only two cosponsors split one Democrat and one Republican, so the record shows too little support to tell how the parties would have lined up.

The exemption threshold would rise from $362,500 to $500,000, freeing small firms from the higher wage rates — though firms newly exempt that were covered in 1988 would still owe the old $3.35 minimum, so some workers at these firms would miss out on the raises.

industries.note: Covered employers would pay up to 90 cents more per hour per minimum-wage worker by 1992, roughly a 27% increase in the wage floor, which is the cost that funds the bill's main benefit to workers.
